metric.why: When interconnection queues stretch to years, on-site generation is the bypass: it trades grid-queue time for fuel logistics, permitting, and backup-capacity obligations. The rise of behind-the-meter builds is a direct gauge of how binding the grid constraint has become.
metric.target: Disclosed in permits, air-quality filings, and operator announcements rather than any central registry.
metric.definition: Dedicated on-site power, gas turbines, microgrids, storage, or eventually reactors, wired directly to the facility rather than drawn through a public grid connection.

reading.body:
Behind-the-meter generation is the clearest available signal that grid interconnection queues have become a hard constraint on data center construction, because operators only absorb the cost and complexity of on-site power when the alternative, waiting in a public queue, is worse.

The logic is straightforward. A facility that generates its own power through gas turbines, microgrids, storage, or dedicated reactors wired directly to the building trades one bottleneck for a set of others: fuel logistics, air-quality permitting, and backup-capacity obligations. Operators accept that trade only under pressure. As the number of behind-the-meter builds rises, it marks, project by project, the places where the interconnection queue has already lost to on-site alternatives as a viable path to powering compute.

The data has a structural gap that matters. No central registry tracks behind-the-meter capacity. The figures surface through permits, air-quality filings, and operator announcements, which means coverage is uneven and the aggregate picture is always incomplete. What this metric can show is direction and precedent, not a reliable total. It also says nothing about whether behind-the-meter generation actually shortens the path to energized compute at scale, or simply relocates the constraint from the grid to fuel supply chains and permitting offices.
